title: From a problem to a model
subtitle: Chapter 1
outcomes: Translate a decision into variables, an objective and constraints.
Use break-even and airline-pricing models to compare alternatives.

topics.title: The management science approach
topics.body:
Management science uses mathematical models and evidence to support decisions. The course also calls it operations research, quantitative methods and business analytics. Pricing, production, logistics, scheduling and ranking all fit this approach.
Start by observing a problem. Define the decision, its boundaries and the organization’s objective. Construct a model; solve it; then implement and check the decision in its actual setting. A mathematically optimal answer is useful only if the model represents the real problem.
A decision variable is something you choose. A parameter is an input you treat as given. The objective measures the result you want to maximize or minimize; constraints define the permitted choices.

sections.title: The steel-product example
sections.body:
A company makes a steel product that sells for $20, costs $5 to produce and needs 4 lb of steel per unit. The firm has 100 lb of steel. Using all available steel gives:
$$\max Z=20x-5x,\qquad4x=100.$$
Solving the displayed equation gives \(x = 25\) units and profit $375.
Modeling note: if steel is merely available rather than required to be exhausted, write \(4x \le  100\) with \(x \ge  0\). Because the contribution is positive and no demand limit is stated, this alternative availability formulation has the same optimum. The equality requires all steel to be used; the inequality merely limits how much may be used.

check.explanation: The model chooses production. Steel availability and selling price are parameters.

topics.title: Break-even: cost, revenue and profit
topics.body:
Fixed cost is the cost that does not change with production volume over the modeled range. Unit variable cost is the additional cost per unit produced.
Read \(c_f\) as “c sub f”: the subscript \(f\) stands for fixed. Read \(c_v\) as “c sub v”: that subscript \(v\) stands for variable. These subscripts are labels, not multiplication and not separate decision variables.
To keep the equations short, write \(F=c_f\) for total fixed cost and \(c=c_v\) for variable cost per unit. Capital \(F\) is an amount of money; lowercase \(c\) is money per unit. For example, a fixed rental bill belongs in \(F\), while material cost for one product belongs in \(c\).
Let \(p\) be selling price per unit and \(v\) the volume of units produced and sold. The standalone variable \(v\) means volume; it is different from the “variable” label in the subscript of \(c_v\). This simple model assumes production equals sales.
In the equations, \(TC\) means total cost, \(R\) means sales revenue, and \(Z\) means profit. All three are amounts of money for the same period:
$$TC=F+cv,\qquad R=pv,\qquad Z=(p-c)v-F.$$
The product \(cv\) is variable cost per unit times the number of units. Similarly, \(pv\) is price times units sold. Subtracting total cost from revenue gives profit.
At break-even, revenue equals total cost, so profit is zero. The subscript \(BE\) stands for break-even: \(v_{BE}\) is the number of units that must be sold to break even. If \(p>c\),
$$v_{BE}=\frac{F}{p-c}.$$
Here \(p-c\) is the contribution per unit: the amount from each sale left to cover fixed cost and then profit. Dividing money by money per unit gives a number of units.
If \(p=c\) and \(F>0\), no finite sales volume covers fixed cost. If \(p<c\), additional sales reduce profit. The model assumes that the chosen volume can be sold at the stated price.

sections.title: Western Clothing Company
sections.body:
For Western Clothing Company, \(F = \$10,000\), \(c = \$8\) per pair and \(p = \$23\) per pair. The break-even volume is \(\frac{10{,}000}{23-8}\approx666.7\) pairs. A whole-unit calculation gives at least 667 sales for nonnegative profit; profit at 667 is $5.
The revenue line starts at zero, and total cost starts at fixed cost. The figures show how changing price, unit cost or fixed cost changes their crossing. Remember that a higher price can make sales harder and can require higher unit cost to improve quality. The interactive controls extend these same equations over user-selected values; they do not estimate demand.

topics.title: Airline demand and a single fare
topics.body:
The airline has 130 seats per departure and a full economy fare of $60. The observed (fare, tickets sold) pairs are (40,55), (50,40), (30,102) and (38,60). Use a fitted demand curve, which need not pass through every observation.
The two displayed branches meet at fare $40 and demand 50. Extending the curve with nonnegative demand and imposing the stated seat limit gives:
$$q(p)=\begin{cases}250-5p&0\le p\le40\\90-p&40\le p\le90\\0&p\ge90.\end{cases}$$
$$s(p)=\min\{130,q(p)\},\qquad R(p)=p\,s(p).$$
The zero-demand truncation and capacity-limited sales formula make the physical bounds explicit. Calculations below use the stated demand curve rather than fitting a new one to the observations.

sections.title: Compare the first three pricing policies
sections.body:
The comparison table reports fare $60, 30 tickets and revenue $1,800 for strategy 1. To fill the plane in strategy 2, solve \(250 - 5p = 130\): fare $24 gives revenue $3,120.
For strategy 3, derive the revenue maximum from the supplied curve. In the uncapped low-price region, \(R = 250p - 5p^2\), with derivative \(250 - 10p\). At \(p = \$25\), sales are 125 and revenue is $3,125. The higher-price branch has its own stationary point at \(p = \$45\), with 45 sales and revenue $2,025. Checking the capacity breakpoint and branch boundaries confirms the best common fare of $25.
The table therefore distinguishes filling all seats from maximizing ticket revenue.

topics.title: Two passenger types and two fares
topics.body:
Separate business travelers who purchase within 14 days of departure from leisure travelers who purchase at least 15 days ahead. Observed business/leisure counts are \(52/3\) at $40, \(40/0\) at $50, \(65/37\) at $30 and \(57/8\) at $38. The last row's type counts disagree with its printed total, as noted below.
The displayed fitted curves are \(q₁ = 90 - p_{1}\) and \(q₂ = 160 - 4p_{2}\). Restricting expected passenger counts to be nonnegative gives:
$$q_1(p_1)=\max(0,90-p_1),\qquad q_2(p_2)=\max(0,160-4p_2).$$
Under one fare, these demands add to the piecewise total-demand curve. For two fares, the two segment revenues share the 130-seat capacity.

sections.title: Find the best two fares
sections.body:
Ignoring capacity initially, business revenue is \(p_{1}\)(\(90 - p_{1}\)), maximized at \(p_{1} = 45\) with \(q₁ = 45\). Leisure revenue is \(p_{2}\)(\(160 - 4p_{2}\)), maximized at \(p_{2} = 20\) with \(q₂ = 80\). The total is 125 passengers, so the capacity constraint does not change these separate maxima.
$$R=45(45)+20(80)=3625.$$
This two-fare policy assumes that the booking restrictions separate the customer types. Allowing every passenger to buy the lower fare would require a different demand model.

topics.title: App specials and a binding seat constraint
topics.body:
The app-pricing model keeps 30 full-fare business passengers paying $60 while an app special attracts additional price-sensitive business travelers. With a fixed leisure fare, the optimum is app fare $40 with 20 app users; optimizing both fares gives app fare $32 with 28 app users and leisure fare $22 with 72 leisure users.
The following is a worked reconstruction of those results from the displayed demand curves. At app fare a, total business demand on \(q₁ = 90 - a\) is split into 30 full-fare customers and residual app demand \(60 - a\). Leisure demand at fare b is \(160 - 4b\). Use \(0 \le  a \le  60\) and \(0 \le  b \le  40\):
$$R=1800+a(60-a)+b(160-4b).$$
$$30+(60-a)+(160-4b)\le130\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a+4b\ge120.$$
This reconstruction assumes that the 30 full-fare passengers do not switch to the app. Allowing these customers to switch would change the demand model and the optimum.

sections.title: Strategy 5: leisure fare fixed at $20
sections.body:
At the fixed leisure fare there are 80 leisure passengers and 30 full-fare passengers, leaving 20 seats for the app. Capacity requires \(a \ge  40\). App revenue a(\(60 - a\)) decreases above its unconstrained maximum at \(a = 30\), so choose \(a = 40\). Revenue is \(1,800 + 40\times 20 + 20\times 80 = \$4,200\), matching the comparison table.
Before adding the app special, the \(\$60/\$20\) pair sells 110 tickets and gives calculated revenue $3,400.

sections.title: Strategy 6: app and leisure fares both variable
sections.body:
The unconstrained choices \(a = 30\) and \(b = 20\) would demand 140 seats, so the capacity constraint binds at the maximum. Substitute \(a = 120 - 4b\):
$$R(b)=-5400+880b-20b^2.$$
The resulting concave quadratic is maximized at \(b = 22\) and \(a = 32\). Counts are 30 full-fare, 28 app and 72 leisure passengers, filling exactly 130 seats. Revenue is \(1,800 + 896 + 1,584 = \$4,280\).

topics.title: Methods and decision support systems
topics.body:
Linear programming uses a clear objective, resource restrictions and known parameters. Probabilistic methods explicitly represent uncertainty. Network methods express relationships as nodes and connections and may be deterministic or probabilistic. Forecasting, inventory models, simulation and multicriteria methods address other structures.
Applications include scheduling, production planning, inventory, pricing, product assortment, capital budgeting, delivery routes and satellite scheduling. The INFORMS journals on applied analytics and data science provide examples of implementation.
A decision support system combines a user interface, databases and management-science models. The decision maker asks “what if?”, compares alternatives and examines sensitivity. ERP systems illustrate how these tools connect across organizational functions and internet-based operations.

topics.title: Case study: making scheduling results usable
topics.body:
The Mitsubishi production-scheduling example illustrates that a solution also needs a usable interface. The old tool needed about two hours to draw 100,000 schedule items, around 13 items per second. Users also needed to move and resize bars, change colors and hatching, show labels and tooltips, change the time scale, open nested rows and resize columns.
The targets were 20,000 items within 10–20 seconds and 100,000 within 0.1–0.2 hour. Instead of preparing the entire chart before displaying anything, compute and draw the requested portion immediately.
A block is a group of schedule data; the view is the visible region; an extended view caches surrounding content. When the view changes, refresh the screen and cache as needed. Modifications update the local scheduling cache and then the database. The interface, drawing/data-management layer and cache separate presentation from server storage.

sections.title: Reported evaluation and its historical setup
sections.body:
The development target used a Core 2 Duo E6550 2.33 GHz PC, 2 GB RAM and Windows XP. The prototype evaluation used a different configuration: a Core 2 Duo P8700 2.53 GHz PC, 4 GB RAM, Windows 7 SP1 and SQL Server 2008. The implementation was in VB.NET.
Five tests were run in each size group. Group A contained about 2,000 rows and 20,000 items, with mean time 17.6 seconds and peak memory below 100 MB. Group B contained about 10,000 rows and 100,000 items, with mean time 131 seconds and peak memory below 200 MB.
The historical prototype achieved approximately 763 items per second and about 60 times the old tool's throughput. These are historical evaluation results with the stated data and hardware, not a current cross-platform benchmark. The implementation lesson is to compute and draw the requested portion of the schedule rather than delay the interface until the whole chart is prepared.

title: Formulate and solve a linear program
subtitle: Chapter 2 · Geometry
outcomes: Build resource, requirement and mixture constraints.
Read a feasible region and distinguish optimal, infeasible and unbounded models.

topics.title: The four assumptions of linear programming
topics.body:
An LP consists of decision variables, a linear objective, linear constraints and variable bounds. The coefficients and right-hand-side values are parameters. To apply it, identify the decision, formulate the model, solve it and implement the result.
Proportionality means a coefficient stays constant as the activity level changes. Additivity means contributions combine by addition, without interaction terms. Divisibility allows fractional variable values. Certainty treats the model’s inputs as known.
$$\max\; c^Tx\quad\text{subject to }Ax\le b,\;x\ge0.$$
Here \(x\) is the vector of decision quantities, \(c\) is the vector of their objective coefficients, \(A\) is the matrix of constraint coefficients, and \(b\) is the vector of right-hand-side limits. The superscript \(T\) means transpose, so \(c^Tx\) is the sum of each coefficient times its corresponding decision quantity, not a power of \(c\). The inequalities apply component by component. These letters are local to this LP model: its \(c\) need not mean the unit variable cost used in the earlier break-even example.
This compact form is an example, not a restriction: an LP can minimize, include equalities or lower-bound requirements, and have other variable bounds. Products of decision variables, squared variables and variable denominators are not linear.
For every variable, state its unit and time period. Every term in one constraint must have the same unit. If actual choices must be whole numbers, an integer model may be required; rounding an LP solution can break feasibility.

topics.title: Beaver Creek: bowls and mugs
topics.body:
Let \(x_{1}\) be bowls per day and \(x_{2}\) mugs per day. Each bowl earns $40, uses one labor hour and 4 lb of clay. Each mug earns $50, uses two hours and 3 lb of clay. There are 40 labor hours and 120 lb of clay available per day.
$$\max Z=40x_1+50x_2$$
$$x_1+2x_2\le40,\qquad4x_1+3x_2\le120,\qquad x_1,x_2\ge0.$$
At (5,10), labor use is 25 and clay use is 50: \(4\times 5 + 3\times 10 = 50\) lb. Both limits are satisfied and profit is $700. The clay total is 50, not 70.
At (10,20), labor use is 50, exceeding 40, so the plan is infeasible even though its nominal profit is $1,400. Feasibility requires every constraint, including bounds, to hold.

sections.title: Slack and binding constraints
sections.body: For an upper-bound resource, slack equals availability minus usage. At (5,10), labor slack is 15 and clay slack is 70. A constraint binds when slack is zero. A feasible plan need not be optimal, and a high objective value does not rescue an infeasible plan.

topics.warning: Each bowl uses 4 lb of clay and each mug uses 3 lb, so clay usage is \(4x_1+3x_2\). At (5,10), this is 50 lb, not 70. Keep both product variables in the clay constraint.

topics.title: Graphical solution and corner points
topics.body:
For two variables, draw each constraint boundary, select the permitted half-plane and intersect all the restrictions with the variable bounds. The pottery diagram shows the resource lines and feasible region. For a ≤ resource constraint, the origin is often a useful test point; a ≥ requirement can select the opposite side.
For the pottery model, the pottery feasible vertices are (0,0), (0,20), (24,8) and (30,0). Their objective values are $0, $1,000, $1,360 and $1,200, respectively. Thus the best plan is 24 bowls and 8 mugs. The redrawn feasible-region diagram and interactive controls use these equations rather than treating imprecise hand-drawn axes as numerical measurements.

sections.title: Worked derivation of the binding intersection
sections.body:
$$x_1+2x_2=40,\qquad4x_1+3x_2=120.$$
Multiply the first equation by four and subtract the second: \(5x_{2} = 40\), hence \(x_{2} = 8\) and \(x_{1} = 24\). Both resources are exhausted.
A constant-profit line has slope −\(c_{1}/c_{2}\). Translating it toward larger profit identifies the last feasible contact. In this bounded pottery polygon, a finite maximum occurs at a vertex; if an objective is parallel to an edge, every point of that edge can tie.

topics.title: Fertilizer: a minimization model
topics.body:
Let \(x_{1}\) be bags of Super-gro and \(x_{2}\) bags of Crop-quick. The purchase costs are $6 and $3 per bag. Their nitrogen contributions are 2 and 4 lb per bag, and phosphate contributions are 4 and 3 lb per bag. The field needs at least 16 lb nitrogen and 24 lb phosphate:
$$\min Z=6x_1+3x_2$$
$$2x_1+4x_2\ge16,\qquad4x_1+3x_2\ge24,\qquad x_1,x_2\ge0.$$
Working from these constraints, the feasible region extends upward and rightward, with lower-boundary vertices (0,8), (4.8,1.6) and (8,0). Their calculated costs are $24, $33.60 and $48. Buy 8 bags of Crop-quick and no Super-gro. 
At that plan, nitrogen supplied is 32 lb, leaving surplus 16 lb, and phosphate is exactly 24 lb. This example has an unbounded feasible region but a finite minimum cost.

topics.title: Multiple optima, infeasibility and unboundedness
topics.body:
Consider changing unit profits, alternate optima, infeasibility and unboundedness. For the pottery calculations here, retain the product-data constraints \(x_{1} + 2x_{2} \le  40\) and \(4x_{1} + 3x_{2} \le  120\), with nonnegative variables. This avoids the repeated printed clay-row typo noted in the pottery topic.
Worked evaluation for profits $70 and $20: the vertex profits are 0, 400, 1,840 and 2,100, so (30,0) becomes optimal. The feasible set stays fixed while the objective selects a different vertex.
For the alternate-optimum example, the objective \(40x_{1} + 30x_{2}\) equals ten times clay usage. Every feasible point on the clay boundary between (24,8) and (30,0) therefore earns $1,200. The diagram is a redraw from those equations; the equality of objective values follows from this calculation.

sections.title: An infeasible model
sections.body:
$$\max Z=5x_1+3x_2,\qquad4x_1+2x_2\le8,\quad x_1\ge4,\quad x_2\ge6.$$
The lower bounds force the left side to be at least 28, contradicting the upper bound 8. Hence this model has no feasible solution, regardless of its objective.

sections.title: An unbounded objective
sections.body:
$$\max(4x_1+2x_2),\qquad x_1\ge4,\quad0\le x_2\le2.$$
Increasing \(x_{1}\) indefinitely stays feasible and increases profit without limit. This is an unbounded maximization problem. It often signals an omitted resource restriction, but whether one is missing must be decided from the original problem.

topics.title: Mixture constraints: chicken and beef
topics.body:
Make a 1,000 lb batch with chicken costing $3/lb and beef costing $5/lb. Requirements are at least 500 lb chicken, at least 200 lb beef, and a chicken-to-beef ratio of at least two to one.
Worked formulation from those stated data: let c and b be pounds of chicken and beef.
$$\min Z=3c+5b,\quad c+b=1000,\quad c\ge500,\quad b\ge200,\quad c\ge2b.$$
Substitute \(c = 1,000 - b\). The constraints give \(200 \le  b \le  1,000/3\), and cost becomes \(3,000 + 2b\). The derived minimum uses \(b = 200\) and \(c = 800\), at cost $3,400.
Because total batch weight is an equality, the feasible mixtures form a line segment. Writing the ratio as \(c \ge  2b\) keeps the formulation linear. The formulation and feasible-region graph use these ingredient requirements.

topics.title: Furniture production and a second graph
topics.body:
Let \(x_{1}\) be doors and \(x_{2}\) windows. Workshop 1 allows four door-hours, workshop 2 allows 12 hours with two per window, and workshop 3 allows 18 hours with three per door and two per window. Profit is $300 per door and $500 per window.
$$\max Z=300x_1+500x_2,\quad x_1\le4,\quad2x_2\le12,\quad3x_1+2x_2\le18,\quad x\ge0.$$
The vertices are (0,0), (4,0), (4,3), (2,6), (0,6). Profits are 0, 1,200, 2,700, 3,600 and 3,000. The optimal mix is two doors and six windows, using all hours in workshops 2 and 3, and leaving two hours in workshop 1.

sections.title: Worked solution of the final graphical exercise
sections.body:
Now solve this two-variable exercise:
$$\max Z=4x_1+5x_2,\quad x_1+2x_2\le10,\quad6x_1+6x_2\le36,\quad x_1\le4,\quad x_1,x_2\ge0.$$
Divide the second constraint by six. Calculating the intersections gives vertices (0,0), (4,0), (4,2), (2,4) and (0,5), with objective values 0, 16, 26, 28 and 25. Thus the derived optimum is (2,4), \(Z = 28\). The \(x_{1}\) upper bound has slack 2.

title: What changes the best decision?
subtitle: Chapter 2 · Sensitivity
outcomes: Find objective-coefficient ranges and local shadow prices.
Distinguish changes in prices, resources and technology.

topics.title: Changing objective coefficients
topics.body:
Find the coefficient ranges using the pottery model with clay constraint \(4x_{1} + 3x_{2} \le  120\).
Here \(c_1\) is profit per bowl and \(c_2\) is profit per mug; subscripts 1 and 2 identify the two products. They are objective coefficients, not total profit or production quantities.
Objective sensitivity asks how much a coefficient can change while the current optimal point remains optimal. For the pottery intersection (24,8), the objective slope must lie between the slopes of its two adjacent edges, −\(1/2\) and −\(4/3\).
$$\frac12\le\frac{c_1}{c_2}\le\frac43\quad(c_2>0).$$
Hold \(c_{2} = 50\): \(25 \le  c_{1} \le  200/3 \approx  66.67\). Hold \(c_{1} = 40\): \(30 \le  c_{2} \le  80\). At either endpoint the current point is still optimal, but an adjacent edge also becomes optimal. These are one-at-a-time ranges; they cannot be applied independently to simultaneous coefficient changes.

sections.title: Derive the coefficient range algebraically
sections.body:
Derive the result from the two binding resource constraints.
The value of one labor hour is \(y_L\) and one pound of clay is \(y_C\). With both pottery products produced, their profits equal the imputed resource costs:
$$y_L+4y_C=c_1,\quad2y_L+3y_C=c_2.$$
$$y_L=\frac{4c_2-3c_1}{5},\qquad y_C=\frac{2c_1-c_2}{5}.$$
Requiring both values to be nonnegative gives the same objective-coefficient range. At the original profits, \(y_L = 16\) and \(y_C = 6\).

topics.title: Cost sensitivity and reduced cost
topics.body:
Use the fertilizer model to find the ranges of bag prices that preserve the current optimum, then interpret the endpoints and reduced costs.
At the fertilizer optimum (0,8), the adjacent edge toward (4.8,1.6) has slope −\(4/3\). The point remains optimal when \(c_{2} \ge  0\) and \(c_{1}\) ≥ (\(4/3\))\(c_{2}\). Holding \(c_{2} = 3\) gives \(c_{1} \ge  4\). Holding \(c_{1} = 6\) gives \(0 \le  c_{2} \le  4.5\).
At \(c_{1} = 4\) or \(c_{2} = 4.5\), a whole boundary edge has the same cost. At \(c_{2} = 0\) and \(c_{1}\) positive, any feasible point with \(x_{1} = 0\) has zero cost. If \(c_{2}\) becomes negative, buying arbitrarily many Crop-quick bags makes this unbounded minimization model decrease without limit.
Reduced cost measures the objective penalty of bringing a currently zero variable into the solution, under the current optimal basis. For Super-gro, one bag costs $6 but replaces $4 of Crop-quick when phosphate remains binding. Its reduced cost is 2, and its cost must fall by $2 before it can enter without worsening the objective.

topics.title: Labor availability and shadow price
topics.body:
How does profit change when labor rises from 40 to 60 hours, falls to 30 hours, or changes slightly around 40 hours?
In this topic \(L\) is available labor hours, \(x_1\) is bowls produced, and \(x_2\) is mugs produced. The notation \(Z^*(L)\) means the greatest achievable profit at labor availability \(L\); the star marks an optimal value, not multiplication.
An RHS sensitivity range preserves the optimal basis, not the numerical values of the decision variables. With pottery clay fixed at 120 lb and labor availability L, solve the same two binding constraints:
$$x_1=48-0.6L,\qquad x_2=0.8L-24.$$
Both variables remain nonnegative for 30 ≤ L ≤ 80. Within this range:
$$Z^*(L)=720+16L.$$
The shadow price is $16 per additional labor hour. From 40 to 60 hours, profit rises by \(20\times 16 = \$320\) to $1,680, with (12,24). At 30 hours, profit is $1,200 with (30,0). This marginal value is local; it is not a purchase recommendation without considering the cost of acquiring more labor.

sections.title: Derived full value function
sections.body:
$$Z^*(L)=\begin{cases}40L&0\le L\le30\\720+16L&30\le L\le80\\2000&L\ge80.\end{cases}$$
For scarce labor, make only bowls because they earn more per labor hour. Above 80 hours, clay limits production to 40 mugs and extra labor has no value. The successive marginal values are 40, 16 and 0; at the breakpoints the left and right derivatives differ.

topics.title: Clay availability and the value of a resource
topics.body:
Study changes in clay availability while holding labor fixed at 40 hours.
Keep labor at 40 hours and let \(C\) be clay availability in pounds. Capital \(C\) is a resource amount here; it is not the lowercase unit cost \(c\) from break-even analysis. As in the pottery model, \(x_1\) counts bowls and \(x_2\) counts mugs. At the intersection:
$$x_1=\frac{2C-120}{5},\qquad x_2=\frac{160-C}{5}.$$
The basis remains feasible for 60 ≤ C ≤ 160, and optimal profit is 640 + 6C. Thus the shadow price at C = 120 is $6 per pound. Reducing clay to 80 lowers profit by $240 to $1,120; the new mix is (8,16).

With little clay, mugs earn more per pound of clay. With abundant clay, labor limits production to 40 bowls. The successive marginal values are \(50/3\), 6 and 0 dollars per pound.

topics.title: Requirement sensitivity in a minimum-cost model
topics.body:
Find how the minimum fertilizer cost and each nutrient’s shadow price change as its required amount varies.
A higher nutrient minimum can raise the least achievable cost. At the current fertilizer solution, nitrogen is already oversupplied; its shadow price is zero. Phosphate binds and its shadow price is $1 per additional pound.
Crop-quick is cheaper per pound of both nutrients. For any nonnegative nitrogen requirement N and phosphate requirement P, the optimal solution uses only Crop-quick:
$$x_1^*=0,\quad x_2^*=\max\left(\frac N4,\frac P3\right),\quad Z^*=\max\left(\frac{3N}{4},P\right).$$
Here \(x_1\) counts Super-gro bags and \(x_2\) counts Crop-quick bags; \(N\) and \(P\) are required pounds of nitrogen and phosphate. A star marks an optimal quantity or minimum cost, and \(\max\) means take the larger of the two expressions.
Hold \(P=24\). Cost stays 24 until N reaches 32, then rises at $0.75 per pound of required nitrogen. Hold N = 16. Cost stays 12 until P reaches 12, then rises at $1 per pound of required phosphate. At N = 16, P = 24, nitrogen can increase by 16 before its shadow price changes; phosphate can decrease by 12 before its current shadow price changes.
For nonnegative requirements, the current nitrogen range is 0–32 and the phosphate range is 12 upward. A solver can report an effectively infinite allowable decrease for a redundant nitrogen lower bound; negative nutrient requirements have no physical meaning here.

topics.title: A new product and a second factory
topics.body:
Should the pottery company introduce a new cup? Compare its profit with the value of the scarce resources it would consume.
A cup would earn $30, using 1.2 labor hours and 2 lb of clay. At the current shadow prices its resources are worth \(1.2\times 16 + 2\times 6 = \$31.20\). Its net contribution relative to these scarce resources is −$1.20, so adding it cannot improve the original optimum.
$$\max40x_1+50x_2+30x_3$$
$$x_1+2x_2+1.2x_3\le40,\qquad4x_1+3x_2+2x_3\le120,\quad x\ge0.$$
At profit 31.20, producing some cups can become an alternate optimum; above that threshold re-solve the model. The shadow-price test is based on the current model and its resource tradeoffs.

sections.title: Willow Valley: model and derived comparison
sections.body:
Willow Valley, a second factory, has profits 48 and 60, labor coefficients 2 and 3, and clay coefficients 4 and 3. Let its labor availability be H:
$$\max Z_W=48y_1+60y_2;\quad2y_1+3y_2\le H,\quad4y_1+3y_2\le120,\quad y_1,y_2\ge0.$$
For \(H \ge  0\), solve as follows. For \(0 \le  H \le  60\), produce (\(y_{1}\),\(y_{2}\)) = (\(H/2\),0). For \(60 \le  H \le  120\), both resource rows bind, giving \(y_{1} = (120 - H)/2\) and \(y_{2} = (2H - 120)/3\). For \(H \ge  120\), produce (0,40).
$$Z_W^*(H)=\begin{cases}24H&0\le H\le60\\480+16H&60\le H\le120\\2400&H\ge120.\end{cases}$$
In the interior range \(60 < H < 120\), Willow’s labor shadow price is 16 and its clay shadow price is 4. At \(H = 40\), the optimum is (20,0), \(Z = 960\). At \(H = 65\), the optimum is (27.5,\(10/3\)), \(Z = 1,520\). These are alternative parameter examples, not two simultaneous labor limits. Compare resource values under the same stated availability rather than comparing unit profits alone.

topics.title: Furniture sensitivity and changing technology
topics.body:
Use the furniture model to find the allowable door-profit range and the marginal value of Workshop 3 time.
For the furniture solution (2,6), hold the window profit at 500. Door profit can range from 0 to 750 while that point remains optimal. At zero, producing fewer doors is equally good; at 750, the workshop-3 boundary edge becomes equally profitable.
Let workshop 3 have H hours. Between 12 and 24 hours, windows remain 6 and doors are \((H - 12)/3\). The profit is \(1,800 + 100H\), so workshop 3 has a shadow price of $100 per hour. Its original 18 hours can decrease by 6 or increase by 6 within this basis.
For H below 12, only windows are made and the marginal value is $250 per hour; above 24, workshops 1 and 2 cap output at (4,6), so extra workshop-3 time has zero value.

sections.title: Changing a resource coefficient: rounded and exact values
sections.body:
If pottery labor per bowl changes from 1 to α, the labor boundary is αx₁ + \(2x_{2} \le  40\). This rotates the line rather than shifting it in parallel. Objective and RHS sensitivity ranges do not answer this change directly.
A rounded coefficient α ≈ 1.33 can suggest the bowl-only point (30,0). At α = \(4/3\) exactly, the solution is (30,0), \(Z = 1,200\). If 1.33 is interpreted literally, the intersection is approximately (29.9252,0.0998), with \(Z \approx  1,201.995\). Preserve the distinction between a rounded coefficient and its exact value. Using 1.33 literally and using exactly four-thirds describe slightly different models.

topics.title: Calculate RHS ranges with slack, surplus and a fixed solution mix
topics.body:
A shadow price is the marginal change in the optimal objective when one right-hand side (RHS) changes and the other model data stay fixed. Assignment 6 adds an algebraic method to the graphical sensitivity lesson.
For a capacity constraint introduce slack; for a minimum requirement introduce surplus:
$$a_1x_1+a_2x_2+s=b,\quad s\ge0,\qquad a_1x_1+a_2x_2-u=b,\quad u\ge0.$$
Slack measures unused capacity; surplus measures how much a requirement is exceeded. At a binding constraint its slack or surplus is zero. Write binding rows directly as equalities.
The solution mix is the set of positive decision and slack/surplus variables. Keep the current zero variables at zero, solve the binding equations in terms of the changing RHS, and require every remaining variable to stay nonnegative.
An RHS is a right-hand-side number in a constraint. A subscript on \(b_i\) identifies constraint \(i\). In the worked examples, \(Z^*\) denotes the optimal objective value as these limits change; the star means optimal, not multiplication.

sections.title: Five steps, and why they work
sections.body: Identify binding rows and the current solution mix. Solve the resulting equations as functions of the RHS. Impose nonnegativity of every decision, slack and surplus variable, and check every original constraint. Substitute into the objective: the coefficient of the changing RHS is its shadow price. With fixed objective and technology coefficients, an optimal basis stays optimal while it remains feasible; this is why the feasibility calculation suffices for RHS sensitivity.

sections.title: A local range is not the entire graph
sections.body: Hold all but one RHS fixed. At a range boundary a variable may reach zero, so the strictly positive mix can change even though the old basis is still valid at that endpoint. Closed validity ranges include their boundary points; unchanged positive mixes and constant marginal slopes apply in their interiors. To cover all nonnegative RHS values, find the adjacent regime and repeat. At a kink, report the left and right marginal values, rather than assert a unique derivative or extend one shadow price forever.

topics.body: Work through pottery and fertilizer examples, changing one right-hand side at a time. Each set of formulas describes its current optimal regime, not every possible limit.

sections.title: Pottery: both resources bind
sections.body:
Maximize \(40x_1+50x_2\) subject to \(x_1+2x_2\le b_1\), \(4x_1+3x_2\le b_2\), and nonnegativity. At \((b_1,b_2)=(40,120)\) the optimum is \((24,8)\), worth 1,360. Solve both binding equations:
$$x_1=\frac{2b_2-3b_1}{5},\quad x_2=\frac{4b_1-b_2}{5},\quad Z^*=16b_1+6b_2.$$
Holding clay at 120 gives \(30\le b_1\le80\) and labor shadow price 16 in the interior. Holding labor at 40 gives \(60\le b_2\le160\) and clay shadow price 6 in the interior. These are separate one-at-a-time ranges; they are not a rectangle in which both RHS values may vary independently.

sections.title: Fertilizer: include a nonbinding row’s surplus
sections.body:
Minimize \(6x_1+3x_2\) subject to \(2x_1+4x_2\ge b_1\), \(4x_1+3x_2\ge b_2\), and nonnegativity. At \((16,24)\), \((x_1,x_2)=(0,8)\) costs 24. The first requirement has surplus 16; the second binds. Keeping \(x_1=0\) gives
$$x_2=b_2/3,\quad u=4b_2/3-b_1,\quad Z^*=b_2.$$
For fixed \(b_2=24\), the nonnegative-RHS validity range is \(0\le b_1\le32\) and the interior shadow price is zero. For fixed \(b_1=16\), the range is \(b_2\ge12\) and the interior shadow price is one. A nonbinding row still matters: its surplus determines where the current regime ends.

topics.title: Build the pottery model in Excel
topics.body:
Computer solvers automate procedures such as the simplex method. Excel Solver and Cardinal Optimizer (COPT) are two tools for this task. Software solves the formulation supplied to it; it cannot check whether the coefficients express the intended business problem.
Separate inputs, decision cells, objective and constraint calculations. In the pottery spreadsheet, C2:D2 contains profits 40 and 50; C3:D3 labor coefficients 1 and 2; C4:D4 clay coefficients 4 and 3. C6 contains 40 and C7 contains 120. C11:D11 holds the changing production quantities.
Set C15 to =SUMPRODUCT(C11:D11,C2:D2), C19 to =SUMPRODUCT(C3:D3,C11:D11), and C20 to =SUMPRODUCT(C4:D4,C11:D11). E19 links to C6 and E20 to C7.
In the demonstrated Solver setup, maximize C15 by changing C11:D11, subject to C19:C20 ≤ E19:E20. Apply nonnegative bounds and use the Simplex LP method. Solve, then independently substitute the returned values into every original constraint.
The expected result is (24,8), profit 1,360, labor usage 40 and clay usage 120. The Answer Report marks both resource constraints binding with zero slack. The original values shown in a report are the initial guesses, not a second optimum.

topics.title: Read sensitivity reports without overextending them
topics.body:
An objective-coefficient range is current coefficient minus allowable decrease through current coefficient plus allowable increase. For pottery bowls, \(40 - 15 = 25\) and \(40 + 26.6667 = 66.6667\). For mugs, \(50 - 20 = 30\) and \(50 + 30 = 80\). Both produced variables have reduced cost zero.
The labor report gives RHS 40, shadow price 16, allowable decrease 10 and increase 40: range 30–80. Clay gives RHS 120, shadow price 6, decrease 60 and increase 40: range 60–160. Within an RHS range, the optimal quantities can change even though the basis is retained; retaining the solution mix does not mean keeping the numerical quantities fixed.
For fertilizer, the changing cells are C9:C10. Minimize C13 = SUMPRODUCT(C2:C3,C9:C10). The nutrient left sides are SUMPRODUCT(C9:C10,D2:D3) and SUMPRODUCT(C9:C10,E2:E3), each constrained above its requirement. The answer is (0,8), total cost 24.
The fertilizer report gives Super-gro reduced cost 2, cost coefficient 6 and allowable decrease 2; Crop-quick coefficient 3, increase 1.5 and decrease 3. Nitrogen’s shadow price is 0 with surplus 16; phosphate’s is 1. Large entries such as 1E+30 denote an effectively unbounded allowable change in the software’s reporting convention.
One-at-a-time sensitivity reports are local and conditional. Integer restrictions, changed coefficients in the constraint matrix or simultaneous data changes can require solving again.

topics.title: Read a solver benchmark critically
topics.body:
The revised Chapter 3 adds a dated solver comparison and a case study about how benchmark selection affects a claim. A benchmark measures particular solver versions on a specified instance set, hardware and stopping rule. It does not establish a universal ordering for every optimization problem.
The LPopt snapshot is dated April 29, 2026 and concerns finding an optimal basic solution on 65 instances. It reports COPT 8.0.0 with score 1.00 and 100% solved. The virtual-best entry is an ensemble reference that selects the best observed solver per instance, rather than a separate solver available for an individual run. Treat this table as the course's historical example, not a current product recommendation.
Compare the complete 240-instance MIPLIB2017 benchmark set with an advertised comparison on 99 selected instances. A selected subset can change measured ratios and need not represent the full benchmark. A 2018 retraction and later benchmark withdrawals illustrate why reproducible comparisons matter. These historical comparisons help evaluate evidence, not proof that one solver will perform best on your model.
When reading a comparison, check the exact instance list, solver versions, machine and thread settings, time limits, aggregation rule and treatment of unsolved instances. Read the solved fraction alongside the aggregate score. Test candidate solvers on representative models of your own before drawing a decision-specific conclusion.

topics.title: LP files and the COPT command-line workflow
topics.body:
The Chapter 3 screenshots use COPT 7.2. The separate September 29 tutorial demonstrates COPT 8.0.7 and a corrected pottery model. Both workflows read a formulation, solve it and export the result. The tutorial introduces programming interfaces as well as the interactive shell and modeling-tool connectors.
Start the interactive shell with copt_cmd. Use pwd to check its working directory, cd to change directories, and dir or ls to list available model files. If a path contains spaces, quote it. A shell can only read a file from a path it can find.
Use read pottery.lp to load the corrected model below, then opt to solve it and writesol pottery.sol to save the result. An optimal result gives \(x_{1} = 24\), \(x_{2} = 8\) and \(Z = 1,360\). Both constraints bind. Substituting the values gives labor \(24 + 2\)(8) = 40 and clay 4(24) + 3(8) = 120.
The course also shows set timelimit 10, writeparam, display/get, optlp, iis, feasrelax, tune and loadtuneparam. Commands and available attributes depend on the installed version. The tutorial points to the copt80 manual in its example installation, while the older Chapter 3 screenshots point to copt72.
An IIS identifies a set of conflicting constraints. Feasibility relaxation changes bounds or constraints to make a problem solvable. Neither operation establishes that a changed formulation still represents the original business requirements. Always inspect solver status before reporting objective values or variable values.

topics.title: Write LP files without changing the model
topics.body:
An LP file is a plain-text optimization model. Maximize or Minimize introduces the objective, Subject To introduces constraints, and Bounds specifies variable bounds. End terminates the file. Use unique constraint names and ordinary comparison operators such as <= and >=.
Variables are continuous and nonnegative unless declared otherwise. A free variable needs an explicit free bound. Generals declares integer variables and Binaries declares variables restricted to zero or one. Those declarations change the mathematical problem. The tutorial's small format example includes both an integer and a binary variable, so it is a mixed-integer example despite being stored in an LP-format file.
On Windows, show file-name extensions before renaming a text document. A file named example.lp.txt is still a text document with a hidden .txt suffix. Use a plain-text editor and separate numeric coefficients from variable names.
The tutorial's parsing example shows why syntax checking alone is insufficient: 4x2 can be read as a variable name rather than four times \(x_{2}\). Its particular malformed file also treats 32 as a variable and combines repeated coefficients on that variable. This is an observed parser trap in the demonstrated file, not a safe way to express a numeric constant.
Export the model and compare its rows and columns with the intended algebra before solving. An MPS export can expose unexpected names and merged coefficients, but changing file format cannot repair an incorrect model on its own.

topics.title: Inspect, export and script a COPT solve
topics.body:
After read pottery.lp, inspect the model before accepting any solve. The corrected pottery formulation has two constraint rows, two variables and four nonzero coefficients in its constraint matrix. Bounds are separate from those two algebraic rows. A column count greater than expected can reveal that a malformed numeric token became a variable.
Use get rows, get cols, get objsense and get elems. Also inspect maxelem, minelem, maxrhs and minrhs. These report model dimensions, objective sense and coefficient or bound magnitudes. Very different magnitudes can motivate checking units and scaling, but an attribute report is not a proof of correctness.
Use writelp pottery-check.lp or writemps pottery.mps to export the loaded model. LP emphasizes human-readable algebra. MPS records named rows and variable-by-variable coefficients. Its ROWS codes N, L, G and E denote the objective, <=, >= and equality rows; COLUMNS holds nonzero coefficients; RHS holds row constants; ENDATA terminates the model. Inspect names and coefficients in either export instead of relying on the original input text alone.
The tutorial contrasts output ordering and parsing behavior of its LP and MPS exports. Those observations describe the demonstrated tools and files; file layout should not be treated as a mathematical property or a universal guarantee for every reader and writer.
After an optimal solve, writesol pottery.sol exports objective and variable values. Exporting LP/MPS does not optimize the problem, while writing a solution file does not establish that the business model was formulated correctly.
For repeatable runs, put commands in an .in file and execute load pottery.in from the COPT shell. The script below adapts the tutorial’s example to the pottery filenames: load the model, set a 10-second limit, solve, then write the solution. A time limit can stop a different problem before optimality, so inspect the final status rather than assuming that every script run found an optimum.

topics.title: Build the same model with the COPT Python API
topics.body:
Build the pottery model directly in Python. Install the interface with pip install coptpy and follow the full COPT setup instructions on Learn. A package installation and the solver's licensing/setup requirements are separate steps.
Create an environment and model, add nonnegative variables, add both resource constraints, set the maximizing objective, choose any parameters and solve. Model construction through expressions avoids manually spelling coefficient-variable tokens in an LP text file.
Check model.status == COPT.OPTIMAL before using the result as an optimum. For the corrected continuous pottery LP, the script returns \(x_{1} = 24\), \(x_{2} = 8\) and objective 1,360. Both variable reduced costs are zero, while the labor and clay dual values are 16 and 6. These are the local shadow prices for this continuous LP and its current basis.
The runnable example names constraints for readable output and raises an error if the solve does not prove optimality. Reduced costs and row duals need the appropriate continuous LP solution; do not reinterpret them automatically as sensitivity reports for an integer model.

code.title: Complete pottery example (requires coptpy)
code.body:
"""Pottery LP from the COPT course tutorial. Requires coptpy."""
import coptpy as cp
from coptpy import COPT

env = cp.Envr()
model = env.createModel("pottery")
x1 = model.addVar(lb=0, name="x1")
x2 = model.addVar(lb=0, name="x2")
model.addConstr(x1 + 2*x2 <= 40, name="labor")
model.addConstr(4*x1 + 3*x2 <= 120, name="clay")
model.setObjective(40*x1 + 50*x2, sense=COPT.MAXIMIZE)
model.setParam(COPT.Param.TimeLimit, 10.0)
model.solve()
if model.status != COPT.OPTIMAL:
    raise RuntimeError(f"No optimal solution: status {model.status}")
print(f"Objective: {model.objval:g}")
for var in model.getVars():
    print(f"{var.name}: value={var.x:g}, reduced_cost={var.RC:g}")
for con in model.getConstrs():
    print(f"{con.name}: dual={con.pi:g}")

topics.title: Product mix: printed shirts
topics.body: Quick-Screen produces front-only and front-and-back printed T-shirts and sweatshirts. Available resources are 500 dozen blank garments of each type, $25,000 for production, 72 processing hours, and one truck with room for 1,200 standard boxes. A standard box holds twelve T-shirts; a sweatshirt box holds twelve sweatshirts but occupies three standard-box spaces. The table gives time, production cost and profit per dozen. The question is how many dozens of each product to make to maximize profit.

sections.title: Derived formulation
sections.body:
Let \(x_{1}\),\(x_{2}\) be dozens of front-only and front-and-back sweatshirts, and \(x_{3}\),\(x_{4}\) the corresponding T-shirt quantities. The following is a continuous LP derived from the stated data.
$$\max Z=90x_1+125x_2+45x_3+65x_4.$$
$$0.10x_1+0.25x_2+0.08x_3+0.21x_4\le72$$
$$3x_1+3x_2+x_3+x_4\le1200$$
$$36x_1+48x_2+25x_3+35x_4\le25000$$
$$x_1+x_2\le500,\qquad x_3+x_4\le500,\qquad x_i\ge0.$$
The constraints represent processing hours, one truck’s capacity, production budget, sweatshirt stock and T-shirt stock. Profit and cost are separate coefficients: maximize the stated profit, while production cost consumes budget. Do not subtract the cost a second time from an already net profit.

topics.title: Diet: lower and upper nutrient limits
topics.body: The breakfast table lists ten foods and their nutrients and costs per stated serving: cup, egg, slice or orange. Minimize cost while providing at least 420 calories, 5 mg iron, 400 mg calcium, 20 g protein and 12 g fiber, and at most 20 g fat and 30 mg cholesterol. The table below gives all food options.

sections.title: Derived continuous-serving model
sections.body:
Let \(x_{i}\) be servings of food i in the table, using its stated unit (cup, egg, slice or orange). Assume continuous quantities, so fractional servings are allowed. Minimize total cost subject to minimum calories, iron, calcium, protein and fiber, and maximum fat and cholesterol.
$$\min\sum_{i=1}^{10}c_ix_i,\qquad x_i\ge0.$$
Using the table’s nutrient coefficients, require calories ≥ 420, iron ≥ 5 mg, calcium ≥ 400 mg, protein ≥ 20 g, fiber ≥ 12 g, fat ≤ 20 g and cholesterol ≤ 30 mg.
For example, the calorie constraint starts \(90x_{1} + 110x_{2} + 100x_{3} + 90x_{4} + 75x_{5}\) and continues with the remaining five table entries. The cholesterol constraint is \(270x_{5} + 8x_{6} + 12x_{8} \le  30\); zero coefficients can be omitted. The objective uses the last column, starting \(0.18x_{1} + 0.22x_{2} + 0.10x_{3}\).
Each nutrient gets its own row and direction. A low-cost food can be unattractive because it consumes a limited upper-bound nutrient such as fat or cholesterol.

topics.warning: This is a derived continuous model: fractional servings are allowed, and every food uses the serving unit listed in the data table. Whole-serving requirements would add integer restrictions.

topics.title: Investment allocation and ratio restrictions
topics.body: Kathleen Allen has $70,000 to invest for one year. The data table gives municipal bonds at 8.5%, CDs at 5%, treasury bills at 6.5% and stock fund at 13%. Municipal bonds may use at most 20% of the total; CDs may not exceed the other three investments combined; CDs and treasury bills together must receive at least 30%; and that group must receive at least 1.2 times the amount in bonds and stock.

sections.title: Derived allocation model
sections.body:
Let \(x_{1}\), \(x_{2}\), \(x_{3}\) and \(x_{4}\) be dollars in municipal bonds, certificates of deposit, treasury bills and the growth stock fund. Annual returns are 8.5%, 5%, 6.5% and 13%, with total capital $70,000.
$$\max Z=0.085x_1+0.05x_2+0.065x_3+0.13x_4.$$
$$x_1\le14000,\qquad x_2\le x_1+x_3+x_4$$
$$x_2+x_3\ge21000,\qquad x_2+x_3\ge1.2(x_1+x_4)$$
$$x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4=70000,\qquad x_i\ge0.$$
The first restriction caps municipal bonds at 20%. The second limits CDs to the other investments combined. The third puts at least 30% in CDs and treasury bills. The fourth is a ratio restriction comparing the two groups, not “20% of total capital.”
The objective is return earned, not final wealth; adding the fixed initial capital would not change the maximizing allocation. The derived LP uses the listed annual returns as fixed objective coefficients.

topics.title: Marketing: maximize exposure within a budget
topics.body: Biggs Department Store wants to maximize advertising exposure using television, radio and newspaper ads. Each advertising option has exposures of 20,000, 12,000 and 9,000 per ad and costs of $15,000, $6,000 and $4,000. Available placements are at most 4 TV commercials, 10 radio commercials and 7 newspaper ads. The agency can produce at most 15 advertisements in total and has a $100,000 budget.

sections.title: Derived LP and the whole-ad distinction
sections.body:
Let \(x_{1}\), \(x_{2}\) and \(x_{3}\) count television commercials, radio commercials and newspaper ads. Exposures are 20,000, 12,000 and 9,000 people per ad; costs are $15,000, $6,000 and $4,000. Budget is $100,000 and production capacity is 15 ads in total.
$$\max Z=20000x_1+12000x_2+9000x_3$$
$$15000x_1+6000x_2+4000x_3\le100000$$
$$x_1\le4,\quad x_2\le10,\quad x_3\le7,\quad x_1+x_2+x_3\le15,\quad x_i\ge0.$$
The model below assumes continuous quantities. If ads must be purchased whole, add integer restrictions. The exposure objective is additive as assumed in the data; it does not account for repeated viewers across advertisements.

topics.title: Transportation: supply, demand and unused capacity
topics.body: Zephyr TV ships televisions monthly from Cincinnati, Atlanta and Pittsburgh to New York, Dallas and Detroit. The data table gives supplies 300, 200, 200, demands 150, 250, 200, and lane-specific unit shipping costs. Find the minimum-cost shipping plan. Supply totals 700 while stated demand totals 600.

sections.title: Derived model: interpret supply as availability
sections.body:
Supply exceeds demand by 100 televisions. Treat warehouse supplies as upper bounds, allowing unused stock at no modeled cost, while meeting each customer’s demand exactly.
Let \(x_{ij}\) be televisions shipped from warehouse i to store j. Warehouse supplies are 300 in Cincinnati, 200 in Atlanta and 200 in Pittsburgh. Demands are 150 in New York, 250 in Dallas and 200 in Detroit.
$$\min\sum_i\sum_jc_{ij}x_{ij}.$$
$$\sum_jx_{1j}\le300,\quad\sum_jx_{2j}\le200,\quad\sum_jx_{3j}\le200.$$
$$\sum_ix_{iA}=150,\quad\sum_ix_{iB}=250,\quad\sum_ix_{iC}=200,\quad x_{ij}\ge0.$$
Supply totals 700 and demand totals 600, so 100 units remain at warehouses. If all warehouse rows were forced to equality without an extra destination, the model would be inconsistent. An equivalent balanced formulation adds a dummy destination with demand 100 and zero shipping cost when unused stock has no modeled penalty.
The objective coefficients are lane-specific: choosing the cheapest warehouse separately for every store can violate warehouse capacities. The model coordinates those shared limits.

topics.warning: Warehouse supplies are upper bounds and unused stock has no modeled penalty. A zero-cost dummy destination is an alternative representation of the 100-unit supply surplus.

topics.title: Blending: percentages become linear constraints
topics.body: The petroleum example blends three components into super, premium and extra motor oil. Component availability is 4,500, 2,700 and 3,500 barrels/day and purchase costs $12, $10 and $14 per barrel. Grade selling prices are $23, $20 and $18. Each grade must have at least 3,000 barrels. Super needs at least 50% component 1 and at most 30% component 2; premium needs at least 40% component 1 and at most 25% component 3; extra needs at least 60% component 1 and at least 10% component 2.

sections.title: Derived LP formulation
sections.body:
Let \(x_{ij}\) be barrels of component i used in grade j, with grades S (super), P (premium) and E (extra). Define \(qⱼ = x_{1j} + x_{2j} + x_{3j}\). Component supplies are 4,500, 2,700 and 3,500 barrels/day; costs are $12, $10 and $14 per barrel. Selling prices are 23, 20 and 18 dollars for S, P and E.
$$\max Z=23q_S+20q_P+18q_E-\sum_j(12x_{1j}+10x_{2j}+14x_{3j}).$$
$$\sum_jx_{1j}\le4500,\quad\sum_jx_{2j}\le2700,\quad\sum_jx_{3j}\le3500.$$
$$q_S,q_P,q_E\ge3000,\qquad x_{ij}\ge0.$$
Super needs \(x_{1S}\) ≥ 0.50qS and \(x_{2S}\) ≤ 0.30qS. Premium needs \(x_{1P}\) ≥ 0.40qP and \(x_{3P}\) ≤ 0.25qP. Extra needs \(x_{1E}\) ≥ 0.60qE and \(x_{2E}\) ≥ 0.10qE.
All these restrictions are linear because q is a sum of variables multiplied only by constant percentages. A percentage refers to its own grade’s total, not total company production.
At the minimum 3,000 barrels of each grade, component 1 needs at least \(1,500 + 1,200 + 1,800 = 4,500\) barrels: its entire supply. Consequently each grade must stay at 3,000 and its component-1 minimum must bind.

sections.title: Derived optimal blend
sections.body:
Use S = (1,500,900,600), P = (1,200,1,500,300), E = (1,800,300,900), in component order (1,2,3). Totals are 4,500, 2,700 and 1,800. Every grade specification holds. Revenue is 183,000 and ingredient cost is 106,200, leaving profit 76,800.
Because component 1 fixes grade totals and component 2 is cheaper than component 3, using all 2,700 available barrels of component 2 minimizes cost. Other allocations with the same totals and satisfied grade restrictions can have the same optimum.

topics.warning: This is a derived formulation and optimum. Grade totals are fixed at the optimum, but component allocations can be nonunique.

topics.title: Multiperiod production and inventory
topics.body: PM Computers seeks a production schedule that meets its orders at minimum cost. Regular production is limited to 160 computers/week, with at most 50 more computers/week from overtime. Unit costs are $190 for regular production and $260 for overtime; holding costs $10/computer/week. Orders in weeks 1–6 are 105, 170, 230, 180, 150 and 250. Initial and terminal inventory must be specified to complete the model.

sections.title: Derived inventory model and boundary assumptions
sections.body:
Let rₜ, oₜ and Iₜ be regular production, overtime production and ending inventory in week t. Assume no initial inventory, no backlogs, and no terminal inventory:
$$I_{t-1}+r_t+o_t=d_t+I_t,\qquad I_0=0.$$
$$0\le r_t\le160,\quad0\le o_t\le50,\quad I_t\ge0.$$
$$\min\;190\sum_{t=1}^6r_t+260\sum_{t=1}^6o_t+10\sum_{t=1}^5 I_t.$$
Impose I6 = 0 and charge holding for inventory carried from one week to the next. These boundary and storage-cost assumptions complete the model.
Week 3 demand exceeds that week’s maximum production by 20; week 6 exceeds it by 40. Earlier inventory is essential. Looking only at total six-week capacity would miss these timing constraints.

sections.title: Derived least-cost schedule under these assumptions
sections.body:
Regular production is 160 every week. Use overtime of 0, 0, 25, 20, 30 and 50. Ending inventories are 55, 45, 0, 0, 40 and 0. Check each balance, for example week 3: \(45 + 160 + 25 = 230\).
Regular production costs 182,400; overtime costs 32,500; holding costs 1,400. Total cost is $216,300. Regular production is cheaper than overtime even with up to five weeks of holding, so all regular capacity is used. The required 125 overtime units are placed as late as the balance and capacity constraints allow.

topics.title: Investment over time: when is money available?
topics.body: Start with $100,000 and a five-year horizon. A can start at the beginning of years 1–4 and returns 15% after two years. B starts at the beginning of year 3, pays 25% at the end of year 5, and is capped at $40,000. C starts at the beginning of year 2, pays 40% at the end of year 4, and is capped at $30,000. Government bond D can be purchased at the beginning of each year and gives a 6% return. The question asks how to maximize the return at the end of year 5.

sections.title: Derived cash-flow model with explicit timing conventions
sections.body:
Use thousand-dollar units. Let Aₜ and Dₜ denote amounts invested at the beginning of year t, and B and C the one-time amounts. For this derived flow model, treat each D purchase as a one-year investment returning principal plus 6%, and make maturity proceeds available for reinvestment at the corresponding year boundary. A 6% return alone does not establish the holding period, so the one-year assumption must be explicit. Assume no borrowing, reserve-cash requirement or transaction costs; all available cash is assigned to projects. The budget constraints below prevent spending a payoff before it arrives.
$$A_1+D_1=100$$
$$A_2+C+D_2=1.06D_1$$
$$A_3+B+D_3=1.15A_1+1.06D_2$$
$$A_4+D_4=1.15A_2+1.06D_3$$

$$W=1.15A_4+1.25B+1.06D_5.$$
A 15% return means a 1.15 maturity multiplier, not 0.15. A flow diagram makes the timing clearer: an A investment skips one intermediate year boundary, while D links consecutive boundaries. With no cash reserve need and positive D returns, unused available funds can be put in D.

topics.title: Data envelopment analysis: relative efficiency
topics.body: Compare Alton, Beeks, Carey and Delancey elementary schools. Inputs are teacher/student ratio, supplementary funds per student and average parent education level; education values mean 12 = high-school graduate and 16 = college graduate. Outputs are average reading, mathematics and history SOL test scores. The goal is to find schools that convert resources into outcomes less efficiently than the others. The full school data are in the table below.

sections.title: Derived DEA formulation and its convention
sections.body:
A single output/input ratio is inadequate when both sides have several measures in different units. DEA searches for nonnegative weights that give each evaluated school its most favorable efficiency score, while preventing any school from scoring above one under the same weights.
For school o, let \(v_{i}\) weight inputs and uᵣ weight outputs. Use an input-oriented, constant-returns-to-scale (CCR) multiplier model:
$$\max\sum_r u_r y_{ro}$$
$$\sum_i v_i x_{io}=1,\qquad\sum_r u_r y_{rj}-\sum_i v_i x_{ij}\le0\quad\text{for every school }j,$$
$$u_r,v_i\ge0.$$
The normalization turns the fractional efficiency ratio into a linear program. Solve separately for each school. A value below one indicates relative inefficiency under this chosen model; a value of one alone is not a claim that every input and output is individually efficient, especially when zero weights or slacks are allowed.
The CCR formulation explicitly assumes constant returns to scale. It is one possible modeling convention. Adding restrictions on weights or choosing variable returns produces a different DEA model.

sections.title: Derived comparison of the observed data
sections.body:
Alton uses no more of any input than Delancey (0.06 vs 0.06; 260 vs 460; 11.3 vs 13.1) and produces at least as much of every output (86 vs 81; 75 vs 73; 71 vs 69). Delancey is therefore dominated in the observed data. DEA is a comparison within the modeled set, not a causal explanation of school performance.
An American Red Cross application integrating Excel, Access and Visual Basic to evaluate chapters with DEA. It illustrates turning many optimization models into a decision-support application.

topics.warning: The CCR formulation assumes constant returns to scale. Different returns-to-scale conventions or restrictions on weights give different efficiency models and can change scores.

topics.title: Uncertain returns and incomplete probabilities
topics.body: Now consider the $100,000, five-year investment problem with random returns. A can start in years 1–4 and pays after two years: 25% return with probability 20%, or 12.5% with probability 80%. B starts in year 3, pays at the end of year 5, and is capped at $40,000: the listed outcomes are a 30% return with probability 40% and 60% with probability 21.67%. C starts in year 2, pays at the end of year 4 and is capped at $30,000: its outcomes are 45% with probability 90% and -5% with probability 10%. D can be bought at the beginning of each year and gives 6%.

sections.title: Derived expected-return calculations
sections.body: A’s two probabilities sum to one, giving expected return 0.2(0.25) + 0.8(0.125) = 0.15. C’s expected return is 0.9(0.45) + 0.1(-0.05) = 0.40. For B, the listed probabilities total only 0.6167, leaving probability 0.3833 unexplained. The listed terms contribute 0.4(0.30) + 0.2167(0.60) = 0.25002, but this is not a complete expectation without the omitted outcome.

sections.title: What is needed to complete the model
sections.body: A stochastic optimization model would need B’s complete distribution, a stated objective for risk, and a description of how returns are jointly realized and observed before later investments. These details are missing from the stated problem. A risk-neutral expected-terminal-wealth model is one possible extension, not the only possible formulation. Later decisions must use only information already observed and cash actually available. Substituting expected multipliers into every cash-balance equation does not automatically produce a valid multistage stochastic plan.

topics.warning: Page 32 leaves 38.33% of B’s probability mass unspecified. Do not invent a missing outcome, silently renormalize the two printed probabilities, or claim a unique stochastic optimum from the incomplete probabilities.

topics.title: Assignment 1: six airport-shuttle pricing policies
topics.body:
A shuttle has 40 seats. Regular tickets are bought less than seven days ahead; advance tickets are bought at least seven days ahead, including exactly seven days, and are nonrefundable and unchangeable. Demand is deterministic, quantities are continuous, operating costs are ignored, and customers do not switch between the regular and advance streams. Choose fares so that all demand is served and total demand is at most 40; there is no additional rationing or overbooking decision.
$$D_W(p)=\begin{cases}54-1.5p&0\le p\le30,\\24-0.5p&30<p\le48,\\0&p>48,\end{cases}\qquad D_A(p)=48-2p,\quad0\le p\le24.$$
The original fares are \(p_W = \$36\) and \(p_A = \$18\). Calculate demands, revenue and load factor for the benchmark; then compare filling capacity, optimizing only the advance fare, optimizing both fares, adding a student fare, and optimizing all three fares. These are derived worked solutions; no official Assignment 1 answer key is available in the synced materials. Related topic: Airline demand, segmentation and advance fares.

sections.title: (a)-(c) Benchmark, fill the shuttle, optimize the advance fare
sections.body: At \(p_W = 36\), regular demand is 6. (a) At \(p_A = 18\), advance demand is 12, giving 18 passengers, 45% load factor and $432 revenue. (b) Filling capacity requires 34 advance passengers, so \(p_A = (48 - 34)/2 = \$7\). Revenue becomes 6(36) + 34(7) = $454. (c) With \(p_W\) fixed, maximize \(216 + p_A\)(\(48 - 2pA\)), subject to \(6 + 48 - 2pA \le  40\). Thus \(p_A \ge  7\); the concave quadratic peaks at \(p_A = \$12\). Advance demand is 24, total demand is 30, load factor is 75%, and revenue is $504. Selling ten fewer seats than in (b) earns $50 more because the retained advance passengers pay a higher fare. Load factor alone is not the revenue objective.

sections.title: (d) Jointly optimize the two fares
sections.body:
On the branch \(p_W \le  30\), use \(p_W = 36\) - (\(2/3\))\(q_W\) and \(p_A = 24 - q_A/2\). Maximize 36qW - (\(2/3\))\(q_W^2 + 24qA - q_A^2/2\), with \(q_W + q_A \le  40\), \(9 \le  q_W \le  54\) and \(0 \le  q_A \le  48\). Capacity binds. Equal marginal revenues give \(q_W = 156/7\) and \(q_A = 124/7\), so \(p_W = 148/7 = \$21.14\) and \(p_A = 106/7 = \$15.14\). Revenue is \(5176/7 = \$739.43\) and load factor is 100%. The chosen regular fare is correctly below 30.
For \(p_W \ge  30\), regular revenue decreases from the branch boundary; the best boundary policy is \(p_W = 30\) and \(p_A = 12\), with \(9 + 24 = 33\) passengers and $558 revenue. For the strictly open branch \(p_W > 30\), $558 is the limiting supremum. Either comparison is below $739.43.

sections.title: (e) Introduce a student fare
sections.body:
The students were already part of regular demand, not an additional population. Nonstudents have DR(pR) = 24 - pR/2 for 0 <= pR <= 48, and students have DS(pS) = 30 - pS for 0 <= pS <= 30; both become zero above their price limits. Student eligibility is checked by ID and nonstudents cannot use the student fare. Equal prices at or below 30 reproduce the first branch of DW; above 30, student demand vanishes.
At pR = 30 and pS = 18, qR = 9 and qS = 12, leaving 19 seats for advance demand. Its unconstrained revenue optimum would sell 24 seats, so the capacity limit binds: \(q_A = 19\) and \(p_A = \$14.50\). Total revenue is \(270 + 216 + 275.50 = \$761.50\), $22.07 above (d). The fixed fares reserve demand of 21 seats regardless of the descriptive ordering of fare choices.

sections.title: (f) Jointly optimize all three fares
sections.body:
Use inverse demands pR = 48 - 2qR, pS = 30 - qS, \(p_A = 24 - q_A/2\) and quantity bounds 0 <= qR <= 24, 0 <= qS <= 30, \(0 \le  q_A \le  48\). Maximize 48qR - 2qR^2 + 30qS - qS^\(2 + 24qA - q_A^2/2\) subject to qR + qS + \(q_A \le  40\). Unconstrained quantities total 51, so capacity binds. Equal marginal revenues are 48 - 4qR = 30 - 2qS = \(24 - q_A = 44/7\).
The optimum is (qR,qS,\(q_A\)) = (\(73/7\),\(83/7,124/7\)), or approximately (10.43,11.86,17.71). Prices are (\(190/7,127/7,106/7\)), approximately ($27.14,$18.14,$15.14). Revenue is \(5365/7 = \$766.43\). This is $27 above joint unsegmented pricing in (d), and $4.93 above fixed segmented fares in (e). Concavity makes the marginal-revenue solution globally optimal. Capacity is allocated until the gain from one more seat is equal across the three eligible groups.

topics.title: Assignment 2: bounded, unbounded and reversed objectives
topics.body: Problems 1, 2 and 4 ask for graphical solutions, including maximization versus minimization. Draw each boundary line, keep the indicated half-plane, and evaluate the feasible vertices. An unbounded feasible region does not by itself imply an unbounded objective; demonstrate an improving feasible direction. All variables are nonnegative. The results below agree with the official key and have been independently recomputed. Related topic: Graphical solution and irregular LP outcomes.

sections.title: Problem 1: a bounded maximum
sections.body:
$$\max Z=5x_1+8x_2;\quad3x_1+5x_2\le50,\quad2x_1+4x_2\le40,\quad x_1\le8,\quad x_2\le10,\quad x_1,x_2\ge0.$$
The feasible polygon has vertices (0,0), (8,0), (8,5.2), (0,10). Their objective values are 0, 40, 81.6, 80. Thus the unique maximum is (8,5.2), \(Z = 81.6\). Draw the boundary from (0,10) to (8,5.2); the first resource and \(x_{1}\) bound meet at the optimum.

sections.body:

The lower boundary vertices are (0,5.5), (4,3.5), and (\(38/7\),\(27/7\)), with \(Z = 11\), 19, and 24. The feasible region extends upward; increasing \(x_{2}\) with \(x_{1}\) fixed remains feasible and increases Z, proving the maximum is unbounded. Reversing to minimization gives (0,5.5), \(Z = 11\).

Let \(x_{1}\),\(x_{2}\) be operating days.

topics.title: Assignment 3: farm profits and a change to corn only
topics.body: The Bradley family has 410 acres and a $52,500 budget. Corn costs $105/acre and earns $300/acre; tobacco costs $210 and earns $520. Tobacco acreage is capped at 100. Define \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) as corn and tobacco acres. Address graphical solution, graphical and algebraic sensitivity, then Excel verification. Related topic: Objective ranges and shadow prices.

sections.title: (a) Model and corner points
sections.body:
$$\max Z=300x_1+520x_2;\quad x_1+x_2\le410,\quad105x_1+210x_2\le52500,\quad x_2\le100,\quad x_1,x_2\ge0.$$
The budget row is equivalently \(x_{1} + 2x2 \le  500\). Vertices (0,0), (0,100), (300,100), (320,90), (410,0) yield profits $0, $52,000, $142,000, $142,800, $123,000. The optimum is (320,90), with land and budget binding and ten acres of unused tobacco quota.

sections.title: (b) Graphical sensitivity and the all-corn threshold
sections.body: The binding boundary slopes are -1 (land) and -\(1/2\) (budget). Optimality requires \(0.5 \le  c_{1}/c_{2} \le  1\). With tobacco profit fixed at 520, corn profit ranges from $260 to $520 (decrease 40; increase 220). With corn fixed at 300, tobacco ranges from $300 to $600 (decrease 220; increase 80). An all-corn plan (410,0) first becomes optimal at corn profit $520. At exactly $520 it shares the optimum with a whole land-binding edge; corn profit strictly above $520 makes all-corn uniquely optimal.

$$Z=142800-80s_L-220s_B.$$

topics.title: Assignment 3: component production and reduced costs
topics.body: Apex produces components A and B. Each A uses two machining units and one finishing unit; each B uses one machining and two finishing. Capacities are 100 and 80, and profits are $50 and $40. Complete the graphical, graphical-sensitivity, algebraic-sensitivity and Excel-report parts. Related topic: Graphical solution and objective ranges.

sections.title: (a) Model and graphical solution
sections.body:
$$\max Z=50x_1+40x_2;\quad2x_1+x_2\le100,\quad x_1+2x_2\le80,\quad x_1,x_2\ge0.$$
The feasible polygon has vertices (0,0), (0,40), (40,20), and (50,0). Their profits are $0, $1,600, $2,800, and $2,500. Thus produce 40 A and 20 B for $2,800/day.

sections.title: (b)-(c) Coefficient sensitivity by slopes and slack algebra
sections.body:
Boundary slopes at the optimum are -2 and -\(1/2\). Thus \(0.5 \le  c_{1}/c_{2} \le  2\). With \(c_{2} = 40\), \(c_{1}\) ranges from 20 to 80; with \(c_{1} = 50\), \(c_{2}\) ranges from 25 to 100. Allowable changes are +/-30 for \(c_{1}\), and decrease 15 / increase 60 for \(c_{2}\).
Introduce machining slack \(s_{1}\) and finishing slack \(s_{2}\):
$$x_1=40-\tfrac23s_1+\tfrac13s_2,\quad x_2=20+\tfrac13s_1-\tfrac23s_2,\quad Z=2800-20s_1-10s_2.$$
For general \(c_{1}\),\(c_{2}\), the slack coefficients are (-\(2c1 + c_{2}\))/3 and \((c_{1} - 2c2)/3\). Both must stay <= 0 for maximization, reproducing \(0.5c2 \le  c_{1} \le  2c2\). Negative coefficients at the stated profits justify optimality.

topics.title: Assignment 5: rank six companies with DEA
topics.body: Each company uses fixed assets, working capital and employees to produce output value and profit-and-tax. The question asks for relative input-to-output efficiency. The assignment does not select a DEA returns-to-scale convention; this worked solution explicitly uses the input-oriented constant-returns CCR model. Related topic: Data envelopment analysis. This is a derived solution verified in COPT and independently with HiGHS, not an official answer key.

sections.title: Input-oriented envelopment formulation
sections.body:
For evaluated company o, use nonnegative reference weights \(\lambda_j\) and input factor \(\theta\). Let \(x_{ij}\) be input i at company j, and \(y_{rj}\) output r.
$$\min\theta;\qquad\sum_jx_{ij}\lambda_j\le\theta x_{io}\ (i=1,2,3),\qquad\sum_jy_{rj}\lambda_j\ge y_{ro}\ (r=1,2),\qquad\lambda_j,\theta\ge0.$$
There is no \(\sum_j\) \(\lambda_j = 1\) constraint in the constant-returns model. Self-reference gives a feasible efficiency of one.

sections.title: Equivalent weight formulation and ranking
sections.body:
Choose nonnegative output weights \(u_{1}\),\(u_{2}\) and input weights \(v_{1}\),\(v_{2}\),\(v_{3}\). For company o maximize \(u_{1}\)*y1o + \(u_{2}\)*y2o, normalize \(v_{1}\)*x1o + \(v_{2}\)*x2o + \(v_{3}\)*x3o = 1, and require every company's weighted output minus weighted input to be <= 0. Each company chooses its most favorable admissible weights. Both LP forms give the same scores.
$$A=B=C=E=F>D,\qquad\theta_D=959/1824\approx0.525767544.$$
D's reference uses \(\lambda_E = 217/1824\) and \(\lambda_F = 973/1824\), with all other weights zero. Its radial input saving is 47.4232%. The five score-one companies remain tied; a stricter ordering would require an additional method or restrictions not specified in the assignment.

$$a_{11}+a_{12}\le800,\quad a_{21}+a_{22}\le1000,\quad a_{11}+a_{21}\le900,\quad a_{12}+a_{22}\le850.$$
$$a_{11}+a_{21}=b_{11}+b_{12}+b_{13},\quad a_{12}+a_{22}=b_{21}+b_{22}+b_{23}.$$
$$b_{11}+b_{21}=500,\quad b_{12}+b_{22}=650,\quad b_{13}+b_{23}=450.$$
Hub capacity counts a unit once; inflow and outflow describe the same unit passing through the hub.

sections.title: (b) One derived COPT optimum
sections.body: Send 750 units P1->T1, zero P1->T2, zero P2->T1 and 850 P2->T2. T1 sends (500,250,0) to C1,C2,C3; T2 sends (0,400,450). Every flow is nonnegative and demand is exact. Cost is 5(750) + 4(850) + 8(500) + 10(250) + 7(400) + 9(450) = $20,500. T2 is full; T1 has 150 spare units. Plant spare capacities are 50 and 150. This is a derived result checked with COPT and HiGHS, not an official answer key.

sections.title: Why the minimum is attained
sections.body: Ignoring capacities, the cheapest full routes to C1,C2,C3 cost $13,$11,$13. Markets C2 and C3 need 1,100 units, but T2 carries at most 850. At least 250 of those units must use T1 at an extra cost of at least $4 each. Every feasible plan therefore costs at least 13(500) + 11(650) + 13(450) + 4(250) = $20,500. The reported plan attains that bound. The 250 T1 units for C2 and C3 can be divided differently while preserving this cost, so optimal flows are not unique.

topics.title: Assignment 6: the marginal value of a distributor quota
topics.body: A concrete plant chooses divisible planning units of basic blocks A and decorative blocks B. Unit contributions are 10 and 35. Five processing capacities and the distributor quota restrict production. The current B quota is 5; study its RHS \(b_6\ge0\) while all processing capacities stay fixed. The table preserves the official problem data. The worked solution below is independently derived, not an official answer key.

sections.title: Formulate and solve the current problem
sections.body:
Let \(x,y\ge0\) be weekly A and B units. Maximize \(Z=10x+35y\) subject to
$$x\le15,\quad x+y\le17,\quad x+2y\le21,\quad x+3y\le27,\quad x+4y\le35,\quad y\le b_6.$$
At \(b_6=5\), the feasible polygon has vertices \((0,0),(15,0),(15,2),(13,4),(11,5),(0,5)\). The optimum is \((11,5)\), profit 285. Heat treatment and the quota bind; all original capacities must still be checked.

sections.title: Derive the full shadow-price graph
sections.body:
For fixed \(y\), positive A profit makes the best A quantity the smallest capacity bound:
$$x(y)=\min\{15,17-y,21-2y,27-3y,35-4y\}.$$
Successive binding rows change at \(y=2,4,6,8\). Profit slopes along these edges are 35, 25, 15, 5, then −5. Hence production stops increasing B at 8 even if its quota increases further. The five nonnegative-quota regimes are in the table. Their value formulas agree at every breakpoint; the shadow-price graph has downward jumps. At \(b_6=8\), the left marginal value is 5 and the right marginal value is 0.

sections.title: Excel Solver verification to carry out
sections.body: Use continuous changing cells A and B, maximize total contribution, add all six constraints and nonnegativity, and select Simplex LP. Solve at quota values 1,3,5,7,9, choosing one interior point from every regime. Expected solutions are \((15,1),(14,3),(11,5),(6,7),(3,8)\), with objectives 185,245,285,305,310. Expected quota shadow prices are 35,25,15,5,0; closed RHS validity ranges are [0,2], [2,4], [4,6], [6,8], [8,∞), restricted to nonnegative quota. Compare the quota row’s allowable increase/decrease with these endpoints. These are independently derived expectations, not reports from an Excel run.

topics.title: Assignment 6: the marginal value of approval slots
topics.body: An advertising agency chooses divisible standard and premium campaign planning units, earning 7 and 13 per unit. Three teams provide the hours in the table. Both campaign types consume one central approval slot. The current approval limit is 11; vary only \(b_4\ge0\). The worked solution below is independently derived.

sections.title: Model and current feasible region
sections.body:
Let \(x,y\ge0\) be standard and premium units. Maximize \(Z=7x+13y\) subject to
$$x+4y\le16,\quad x+3y\le14,\quad x+2y\le13,\quad x+y\le b_4.$$
At \(b_4=11\), the polygon vertices are \((0,0),(11,0),(9.5,1.5),(8,2),(0,4)\). The optimum is \((9.5,1.5)\), contribution 86. Content editing and approvals bind.

sections.title: Follow the binding constraints as approvals increase
sections.body:
While approvals bind, put \(x=b_4-y\), so \(Z=7b_4+6y\). The largest feasible premium quantity is constrained by
$$y\le b_4,\quad y\le(16-b_4)/3,\quad y\le(14-b_4)/2,\quad y\le13-b_4.$$
These bounds become active in order, giving breakpoints 4,10,12,13 and the table’s formulas. Once approvals reach 13, \((13,0)\) earns 91 and more approvals have no value. For example, the final publishing inequality also proves \(7x+13y\le7(x+2y)\le91\). Interior shadow prices are 13,5,4,1,0. Do not assign one differentiable slope at a breakpoint.

sections.body: Use Simplex LP with continuous nonnegative variables and request a Sensitivity Report after each solve. Interior approval values 2,7,11,12.5,14 should produce (A,B) = (0,2),(4,3),(9.5,1.5),(12,0.5),(13,0), objectives 26,67,86,90.5,91, and approval shadow prices 13,5,4,1,0. Corresponding closed RHS validity ranges, restricted to nonnegative approvals, are [0,4], [4,10], [10,12], [12,13], [13,∞).
